title: Light & optics
subtitle: An introductory path from rays to detection
prerequisites: Mathematical toolkit, Electricity & magnetism, Vibrations & waves. Local mathematical bridges are taught before use; advanced topics retain their stated prerequisites.

lessons.title: One wave, many wavelengths
lessons.idea: Visible light is a small part of the electromagnetic spectrum.
body: A radio wave and green light are both travelling electromagnetic disturbances. The labels describe ranges of frequency, not different rules for empty space. Your eyes detect only a limited range; invisible does not mean absent.

Frequency counts repeats each second. Wavelength measures the distance between matching parts of a repeating wave. In vacuum their product is the speed of light. Shorter vacuum wavelength therefore means higher frequency.

Use a vacuum wavelength when you label a spectral band. Inside ordinary transparent material, frequency stays fixed at a stationary boundary while wavelength usually changes. A colour name is not a complete physical measurement.
lessons.terms: c: Vacuum light speed (m/s). Use 3.00×10⁸ m/s for rounded examples. f: Frequency (Hz). One hertz means one repeat per second. λ₀: Vacuum wavelength (m). Greek lambda names wavelength; zero marks vacuum.

equationGuide.meaning: The distance per repeat multiplied by repeats per second gives distance per second.

symbols.name: Vacuum light speed
symbols.description: Use 3.00×10⁸ m/s for rounded examples.

symbols.name: Frequency
symbols.description: One hertz means one repeat per second.

symbols.name: Vacuum wavelength
symbols.description: Greek lambda names wavelength; zero marks vacuum.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: A wave has vacuum wavelength 600 nm; nm means 10⁻⁹ metre.
Convert: 600 nm = 6.00×10⁻⁷ m.
Divide c by wavelength: f = 5.00×10¹⁴ Hz.

check.prompt: Another vacuum wave has twice that wavelength. What changes?
explanations: Correct. The vacuum speed stays c, so the product fλ₀ must stay fixed.
Not quite. The vacuum speed stays c, so the product fλ₀ must stay fixed.
Not quite. The vacuum speed stays c, so the product fλ₀ must stay fixed.

apply.title: Explain your prediction
apply.text: Can an invisible infrared source carry energy? Explain without relying on what eyes see.
apply.answer: Yes. Infrared is electromagnetic radiation outside the eye’s response range. Visibility is a property of the detector and wavelength range, not a test for whether a wave transports energy.

lessons.limits: Vacuum relation; material dispersion and detector responses require their own models. This is not a radiation-safety guide.

visual.title: Follow the physical story
visual.caption: Compare distances for one repeat, not the colour labels.

glossary.definition: A way to arrange radiation by frequency or wavelength.

practice.prompt: Use c=3.00×10⁸ m/s and λ₀=750 nm.
practice.reasoning: 3.00×10⁸ divided by 750×10⁻⁹ gives 4.00×10¹⁴ Hz. The entry tolerance permits rounding; it is not measurement uncertainty.

lessons.title: A ray points across a wavefront
lessons.idea: A ray is a direction marker, not a little glowing wire.
body: Imagine drawing a line through all the crests of a water ripple at one instant. That is a wavefront: places with the same phase, or same position in a repeat. Light also has wavefronts even when we cannot see each repeat.

In a uniform isotropic material, rays point normal to wavefronts. Normal means at a right angle. A plane wave has flat wavefronts and parallel rays; a small source can produce nearly spherical wavefronts and spreading rays.

The distance between consecutive wavefronts is a wavelength. Rays throw away the phase information. They are useful for tracing where an image forms, but cannot by themselves predict bright and dark interference fringes.
lessons.terms: v: Wavefront speed (m/s). The speed in the chosen uniform medium. λ: Wavefront spacing (m). Distance between consecutive equal-phase fronts. Δt: Time between passing fronts (s). Delta means a difference; here this is one period.

equationGuide.meaning: A wavefront moves one wavelength in one period.

symbols.name: Wavefront speed
symbols.description: The speed in the chosen uniform medium.

symbols.name: Wavefront spacing
symbols.description: Distance between consecutive equal-phase fronts.

symbols.name: Time between passing fronts
symbols.description: Delta means a difference; here this is one period.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: Let wavefront spacing be 0.40 μm; μm means 10⁻⁶ metre.
Let the passing time be 2.0×10⁻¹⁵ s.
The speed is 0.40×10⁻⁶ divided by 2.0×10⁻¹⁵ = 2.0×10⁸ m/s.

check.prompt: Flat wavefronts tilt but keep their spacing. What happens to the rays?
options: They turn to remain normal to the fronts
They stay in the old direction
explanations: Not quite. The ray direction follows the normal, not the edge of the drawing.
Correct. The ray direction follows the normal, not the edge of the drawing.
Not quite. The ray direction follows the normal, not the edge of the drawing.

apply.title: Explain your prediction
apply.text: Why would a ray sketch alone miss a dark stripe made by two overlapping beams?
apply.answer: The sketch gives directions but not the relative phase. A dark stripe depends on the fields arriving with cancelling phases. That information requires a wave description.

lessons.limits: Normal ray direction here assumes isotropic media; anisotropic crystals can have energy flow not parallel to the wavevector.

visual.title: Follow the physical story
visual.caption: Wavefront lines and ray arrows encode different information.

glossary.definition: A direction perpendicular to a surface.
Position within a repeating cycle.

lessons.title: Check the size before drawing rays
lessons.idea: Ray optics works best when relevant structures are large compared with wavelength.
body: A doorway is huge compared with a light wavelength. A very narrow slit may not be. At an edge, the wave spreads into directions that a straight-ray shadow would miss.

Compare wavelength with the smallest feature that matters to your question. A small ratio supports ray tracing away from sharp edges and focal details. It does not guarantee that an image has zero blur.

Even a large lens makes a finite diffraction spot near focus. Use rays for the approximate image position and waves for the smallest resolvable detail. Choosing a model is choosing which effects may be neglected.
lessons.terms: ε: Scale ratio (no unit). Greek epsilon is the wavelength-to-feature ratio. λ: Wavelength in the medium (m). Use the wavelength where the structure acts. a: Relevant feature size (m). Positive width, aperture or curvature scale.

equationGuide.meaning: A small ratio means many wavelengths fit across the feature.

symbols.name: Scale ratio
symbols.description: Greek epsilon is the wavelength-to-feature ratio.

symbols.name: Wavelength in the medium
symbols.description: Use the wavelength where the structure acts.

symbols.name: Relevant feature size
symbols.description: Positive width, aperture or curvature scale.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: Take λ=0.50 μm and a=1.0 mm.
Convert a to 1000 μm so both lengths use the same unit.
The ratio is 0.00050: rays may locate an image, but diffraction still matters for its fine structure.

check.prompt: Keeping wavelength fixed, make the aperture 100 times narrower. What happens?
options: The ratio grows 100 times, so diffraction is harder to neglect
explanations: Not quite. Dividing by a smaller feature increases λ/a.
Not quite. Dividing by a smaller feature increases λ/a.
Correct. Dividing by a smaller feature increases λ/a.

apply.title: Explain your prediction
apply.text: Can a small λ/a justify using rays to calculate an interference minimum?
apply.answer: No. The requested quantity is itself a phase-cancellation effect. A small geometric ratio may justify ray paths, but phases must still be tracked to predict interference.

lessons.limits: This is a scale diagnostic, not a universal error bound. Caustics, edges and coherent interference need wave analysis.

visual.title: Follow the physical story
visual.caption: Ask both how large the device is and what you want to predict.

glossary.definition: Wave spreading caused by finite openings or obstacles.

lessons.title: The same power can cover more area
lessons.idea: Irradiance is received power per area, not total beam power.
body: A torch can spread its light over a larger patch. The total arriving power may stay the same while each square metre receives less. Here the symbol I means irradiance, often called intensity in introductory optics.

For a uniform patch, divide received power by its area. If brightness varies across the patch, this gives only the average. A detector needs the power actually landing on its sensitive area, not the source’s total output.
Area grows as the square of a circle’s radius. Doubling a uniform spot radius makes four times the area, so the same power gives one quarter the irradiance.
lessons.terms: I: Average irradiance (W/m²). A watt per square metre is power per receiving area. P: Received power (W). One watt is one joule per second. A: Illuminated area (m²). Use the area on the receiving surface. r: Circular spot radius (m). Half the spot diameter. π: Circle constant (no unit). Approximately 3.14159; r² means r multiplied by itself.

equationGuide.meaning: Power is shared over the receiving area; spreading it lowers the average.

symbols.description: A watt per square metre is power per receiving area.

symbols.name: Received power
symbols.description: One watt is one joule per second.

symbols.name: Illuminated area
symbols.description: Use the area on the receiving surface.

symbols.name: Circular spot radius
symbols.description: Half the spot diameter.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: A uniform beam delivers 0.020 W over 0.010 m².
Divide power by area: 0.020/0.010 = 2.0 W/m².
Spread the same power over 0.040 m²: the average becomes 0.50 W/m².

check.prompt: A detector area halves inside an unchanged uniform beam. What happens to collected power?
options: It stays fixed because irradiance is fixed
explanations: Correct. Power equals irradiance times collecting area when the whole detector is illuminated.
Not quite. Power equals irradiance times collecting area when the whole detector is illuminated.
Not quite. Power equals irradiance times collecting area when the whole detector is illuminated.

apply.title: Explain your prediction
apply.text: Why is a source’s watt rating insufficient to predict a sensor signal?
apply.answer: Some power may miss the sensor or be absorbed on the way. You need the spatial distribution at the sensor, its sensitive area and its wavelength-dependent response, not just emitted power.

lessons.limits: Uniform or area-averaged illumination; no eye-safety inference from these examples.

visual.title: Follow the physical story
visual.caption: Separate a total flow from the amount received per area.

glossary.definition: Optical power received per unit surface area.

practice.prompt: A uniform 0.030 W beam covers 0.015 m².
practice.reasoning: Divide 0.030 W by 0.015 m². The entry tolerance permits rounding; it is not measurement uncertainty.

lessons.title: Measure from the normal, not the mirror
lessons.idea: Reflection uses equal angles measured from the surface normal.
body: Draw a line at right angles to the mirror at the point where light arrives. This normal is the reference for both the incoming and outgoing ray. Angles measured from the surface are their complements, not the angles in the reflection law.
The incoming ray, reflected ray and normal lie in one plane for a smooth isotropic mirror. The incident and reflected angles have equal size on opposite sides of the normal.
A curved mirror has a different normal at each point. Applying the same local rule across its surface can bring nearby rays together or spread them apart.
lessons.terms: θᵢ: Incident angle (degrees or rad). Measured between the incoming ray direction toward the surface and the normal line. θᵣ: Reflected angle (same angle unit). Measured between the outgoing ray and normal; subscripts identify incoming and reflected.

equationGuide.meaning: The ray leaves at the same angular distance from the normal as it arrived.

symbols.name: Incident angle
symbols.description: Measured between the incoming ray direction toward the surface and the normal line.

symbols.name: Reflected angle
symbols.description: Measured between the outgoing ray and normal; subscripts identify incoming and reflected.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: An incoming ray is 25° above the mirror surface.
Its angle from the normal is 90°−25°=65°.
The reflected ray is also 65° from the normal, or 25° above the surface.

check.prompt: A ray arrives 40° from the normal. Which reflected direction obeys the law?
options: 40° from the normal on the outgoing side
explanations: Not quite. Use the normal for both angles; changing the reference changes the number.
Correct. Use the normal for both angles; changing the reference changes the number.
Not quite. Use the normal for both angles; changing the reference changes the number.

apply.title: Explain your prediction
apply.text: Why does rough paper not show a clear mirror image even though reflection still occurs?
apply.answer: Tiny surface patches have different normals, so their reflected directions spread out. The local reflection rule can still apply, but the many directions do not form the orderly image of a smooth mirror.

lessons.limits: Specular reflection from a smooth surface; polarization-dependent amplitudes are not calculated here.

visual.title: Follow the physical story
visual.caption: Choose the normal before placing either angle.

glossary.definition: Orderly reflection from a surface smooth on the relevant wavelength scale.

lessons.title: A boundary changes direction and wavelength
lessons.idea: Snell’s law compares angles using refractive indices.
body: At a stationary boundary, consecutive crests must join consistently on both sides. Frequency therefore stays the same. Wave speed and wavelength can change, so the fronts turn.

Refractive index is vacuum light speed divided by phase speed. In ordinary transparent materials at the chosen wavelength, a larger index means a smaller phase speed. The angle in Snell’s law is always measured from the normal.
Entering a higher-index medium bends a non-normal ray toward the normal. At normal incidence there is no turn. Some light can also reflect; a direction law does not tell how much is transmitted.
lessons.equation: n₁ sinθ₁ = n₂ sinθ₂; n = c/v
lessons.terms: n₁, n₂, n: Refractive indices (no unit). Subscripts label the incident and transmitted media at the stated frequency. θ₁, θ₂: Angles to the normal (degrees or rad). Use the same angle convention in both media. c, v: Vacuum and material phase speeds (m/s). Their ratio defines index; sin means sine.

equationGuide.meaning: The index-weighted sideways part of the ray direction matches across the boundary.

symbols.name: Refractive indices
symbols.description: Subscripts label the incident and transmitted media at the stated frequency.

symbols.name: Angles to the normal
symbols.description: Use the same angle convention in both media.

symbols.name: Vacuum and material phase speeds
symbols.description: Their ratio defines index; sin means sine.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: Light enters index 1.50 glass from index 1.00 air at 30° to the normal.
The transmitted sine is (1.00/1.50)sin 30° = 1/3.
The transmitted angle is arcsin(1/3) ≈19.47°; arcsin reverses sine on the physical 0°–90° branch.

check.prompt: At the same boundary the ray enters straight along the normal. What happens?
options: Its direction stays straight while speed and wavelength change
explanations: Not quite. Zero incident angle gives zero transmitted angle; a stationary boundary preserves frequency.
Not quite. Zero incident angle gives zero transmitted angle; a stationary boundary preserves frequency.
Correct. Zero incident angle gives zero transmitted angle; a stationary boundary preserves frequency.

apply.title: Explain your prediction
apply.text: Why must the index be specified at a wavelength?
apply.answer: Materials generally have different phase speeds at different frequencies. Using a single index for all colours can hide dispersion and give the wrong transmitted angle.

lessons.limits: Flat stationary boundary, transparent isotropic media, propagating transmitted ray. Negative-index or absorbing media need more care.

visual.title: Follow the physical story
visual.caption: Track quantities separately at the boundary.

glossary.definition: Ratio of vacuum speed to material phase speed.

practice.prompt: Index 1.00 to 1.25, incident angle 30°. Enter the sine, not the angle.
practice.reasoning: (1.00/1.25)×0.5=0.4. The entry tolerance permits rounding; it is not measurement uncertainty.

lessons.title: When no transmitted ray angle exists
lessons.idea: Total internal reflection requires travel from higher to lower index.
body: When light tries to leave a higher-index material, the transmitted ray bends away from the normal. Increasing the incident angle eventually makes the transmitted ray run along the boundary.
At that critical angle, the transmitted sine is one. Beyond it, Snell’s law would demand a sine larger than one, so there is no travelling transmitted ray into the second ideal medium.

The field does not suddenly vanish beyond the boundary. An evanescent field extends a short distance and decays. A nearby second material can interact with it, so total reflection is not a universal rule for every layered device.
lessons.terms: θc: Critical incident angle (degrees or rad). Angle to the normal at the onset of grazing transmission. n₁, n₂: Incident and outside indices (no unit). Both are positive here; n₁ must exceed n₂.

equationGuide.meaning: The largest possible transmitted sine determines the critical incident angle.

symbols.name: Critical incident angle
symbols.description: Angle to the normal at the onset of grazing transmission.

symbols.name: Incident and outside indices
symbols.description: Both are positive here; n₁ must exceed n₂.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: Light travels from index 1.50 glass toward index 1.00 air.
The critical sine is 1/1.5=2/3.
The critical angle is about 41.81°; an incident 50° ray has total internal reflection in this ideal two-medium model.

check.prompt: From air into glass, can increasing the angle produce this same total internal reflection?
options: No; the incident index is smaller
explanations: Correct. The critical-angle construction requires n₁>n₂.
Not quite. The critical-angle construction requires n₁>n₂.
Not quite. The critical-angle construction requires n₁>n₂.

apply.title: Explain your prediction
apply.text: Why is “no light field outside” an incorrect description of total internal reflection?
apply.answer: There is an evanescent field outside even without a propagating transmitted beam. Its decay and possible coupling to nearby structures matter in waveguides and frustrated total internal reflection.

lessons.limits: Lossless positive-index media and an isolated boundary; absorption or nearby boundaries change the energy accounting.

visual.title: Follow the physical story
visual.caption: Check the index order before calculating an angle.

glossary.definition: A field that decays away from an interface rather than carrying a travelling wave into that region.

lessons.title: Different colours can turn by different amounts
lessons.idea: Dispersion means refractive index depends on frequency.
body: A prism can separate colours because its index is not exactly the same for every frequency. The first and second boundaries both matter; the prism is not creating new frequencies from white light.

For each colour, use its own index in the refraction calculation. In many transparent visible-band glasses, shorter wavelengths have a larger index and bend more toward a normal on entry. This trend is not universal near absorption bands.

A pulse contains several frequencies. Their phases can advance differently, so pulse shape and arrival timing need more than a single phase index. The wave course’s group-speed distinction becomes important.
lessons.terms: λ: Wavelength in material (m). Distance between fronts inside the material. λ₀: Vacuum wavelength (m). Labels the unchanged optical frequency. n(λ₀): Index at that vacuum wavelength (no unit). Parentheses mean the index is a function of wavelength.

equationGuide.meaning: At fixed frequency, the material wavelength shrinks by the phase-index factor.

symbols.name: Wavelength in material
symbols.description: Distance between fronts inside the material.

symbols.name: Vacuum wavelength
symbols.description: Labels the unchanged optical frequency.

symbols.name: Index at that vacuum wavelength
symbols.description: Parentheses mean the index is a function of wavelength.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: For one colour let λ₀=600 nm and n=1.50.
The material wavelength is 600/1.50=400 nm.
For another colour do not reuse 1.50 unless the material data justify it.

check.prompt: Two colours enter the same glass at the same angle; blue has the larger index. Which bends closer to the normal?
explanations: Not quite. Snell’s law gives a smaller transmitted sine for the larger index.
Correct. Snell’s law gives a smaller transmitted sine for the larger index.
Not quite. Snell’s law gives a smaller transmitted sine for the larger index.

apply.title: Explain your prediction
apply.text: Would equal phase indices at one frequency prove a short pulse propagates identically in two materials?
apply.answer: No. A pulse samples nearby frequencies. Different frequency dependence can give different group delays and spreading even when the phase index matches at one frequency.

lessons.limits: Transparent-band dispersion only; strong absorption and broadband pulse distortion require fuller material response models.

visual.title: Follow the physical story
visual.caption: Use one material property value for each frequency.

glossary.definition: Dependence of wave propagation on frequency.

lessons.title: An image can be a meeting or an apparent origin
lessons.idea: A real image forms where rays actually meet; a virtual image is where they appear to come from.
body: Place a small arrow in front of an optical device. Trace several rays from just its tip. If the outgoing rays meet, a screen at that meeting place can catch a sharp image of the tip.

If the outgoing rays spread apart, extend them backward as dotted construction lines. Their backward meeting point can locate a virtual image. No light is travelling along those dotted extensions behind a mirror.
Your eye can focus either kind of incoming ray bundle onto its retina. “Virtual” does not mean imaginary or invisible; it says how the rays from the device are arranged.
lessons.terms: dᵢ: Signed image distance (m or cm). For a lens, positive is the outgoing side; for a mirror, positive is the reflecting side. Use the appropriate device convention.

equationGuide.meaning: The sign records whether the outgoing rays truly meet or only their backward extensions meet.

symbols.name: Signed image distance
symbols.description: For a lens, positive is the outgoing side; for a mirror, positive is the reflecting side. Use the appropriate device convention.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: Parallel rays through a converging lens meet 15 cm behind it.
That is a real image with dᵢ=+15 cm in the lens convention.
A screen there intercepts the rays; a backward extension alone would not put light on a screen.

check.prompt: A mirror makes rays appear to start behind its surface. Can a screen placed behind an opaque mirror catch that image directly?
options: Yes; every visible image exists on a screen
Only if the screen is white
No; the backward extensions are not travelling rays
explanations: Not quite. The virtual image marks an apparent origin, not an actual transmitted ray crossing.
Not quite. The virtual image marks an apparent origin, not an actual transmitted ray crossing.
Correct. The virtual image marks an apparent origin, not an actual transmitted ray crossing.

apply.title: Explain your prediction
apply.text: How can you see a virtual image if no rays meet at its apparent position?
apply.answer: Rays still enter your eye from the device. The eye focuses those rays onto the retina, and their directions indicate an apparent source position. The virtual image need not itself be a place where energy converges.

lessons.limits: Paraxial image terminology; extended objects and aberrations can prevent a single exact meeting point.

visual.title: Follow the physical story
visual.caption: Use solid lines for rays and dotted lines only for construction.

glossary.definition: Apparent source found by extending outgoing rays backward.

lessons.title: Curved mirrors use changing normals
lessons.idea: A spherical mirror behaves approximately like a focusing element near its axis.
body: A plane mirror produces an upright virtual image as far behind the plane as the object is in front. A curved mirror changes its normal across the surface, so different rays can converge or diverge.

For a spherical mirror, the paraxial focal length is half the signed radius of curvature. Concave focusing mirrors have positive focal length in our real-is-positive convention; convex mirrors have negative focal length.

Paraxial means rays close to the axis and at small angles. Rays far from the axis of a spherical mirror need not share the same focus. This defect is spherical aberration, not a failure of local reflection.
lessons.terms: f, R: Signed focal length and curvature radius (m or cm). Concave is positive; convex is negative in this convention. dₒ, dᵢ: Object and image distances (same length unit). A real object in front has dₒ>0; a real reflected image in front has dᵢ>0.

equationGuide.meaning: Curvature sets an approximate focus; object distance then sets where the reflected rays meet.

symbols.name: Signed focal length and curvature radius
symbols.description: Concave is positive; convex is negative in this convention.

symbols.name: Object and image distances
symbols.description: A real object in front has dₒ>0; a real reflected image in front has dᵢ>0.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: A concave mirror has R=40 cm, hence f=20 cm.
For a real object 60 cm in front, 1/dᵢ=1/20−1/60=1/30 per cm.
The image is real at dᵢ=30 cm in front of the mirror.

check.prompt: A convex mirror views a real object. Can its negative focal length give a positive real image distance here?
explanations: Correct. Both terms make 1/dᵢ negative for negative f and positive dₒ.
Not quite. Both terms make 1/dᵢ negative for negative f and positive dₒ.
Not quite. Both terms make 1/dᵢ negative for negative f and positive dₒ.

apply.title: Explain your prediction
apply.text: Why can narrowing the illuminated region of a spherical mirror improve its geometric focus?
apply.answer: It removes the far-from-axis rays that violate the paraxial approximation most strongly. It can reduce spherical aberration, although the smaller aperture also increases diffraction spreading.

lessons.limits: Spherical paraxial mirror in one uniform medium; not exact for large ray angles.

visual.title: Follow the physical story
visual.caption: A surface shape changes normals, not the reflection law.

glossary.definition: Close to the optical axis and with small ray angles.

lessons.title: Keep the signs when a lens makes an image
lessons.idea: The thin-lens equation predicts both real and virtual image positions.
body: Treat the lens as one thin plane. For a real object on the incoming side, dₒ is positive. For the outgoing rays, dᵢ is positive if they meet on the far side, and negative if only their backward extensions meet on the object side.
A converging lens has positive focal length f. Subtract the reciprocal object distance from the reciprocal focal length, then invert to find the image distance. Use one length unit throughout.

If the object sits exactly one focal length away, the outgoing rays are parallel. The reciprocal image distance is zero: there is no finite image plane. This is not a prediction of infinite brightness.
Moving the object inside the focal distance makes dᵢ negative. The lens then produces a virtual image even though it is still a converging lens.
lessons.terms: f: Signed focal length (m or cm). Positive for a converging lens. dₒ: Object distance (same length unit). Positive for the real object on the incoming side. dᵢ: Signed image distance (same length unit). Positive for a real outgoing-side image; negative for a virtual object-side image.

equationGuide.meaning: The reciprocal distances balance; crossing the focal object position changes the image from real to virtual.

symbols.name: Signed focal length
symbols.description: Positive for a converging lens.

symbols.name: Object distance
symbols.description: Positive for the real object on the incoming side.

symbols.name: Signed image distance
symbols.description: Positive for a real outgoing-side image; negative for a virtual object-side image.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: Take f=10 cm and dₒ=30 cm.
Then dᵢ=(10×30)/(30−10)=15 cm: a real image.
Move the object to 5 cm: dᵢ=(10×5)/(5−10)=−10 cm, a virtual image.

check.prompt: With f=10 cm and dₒ=10 cm, where is the image?
options: There is no finite image plane; outgoing rays are parallel
explanations: Not quite. The denominator dₒ−f is zero, so the finite-distance formula cannot be used.
Correct. The denominator dₒ−f is zero, so the finite-distance formula cannot be used.
Not quite. The denominator dₒ−f is zero, so the finite-distance formula cannot be used.

apply.title: Explain your prediction
apply.text: Would calling a converging lens “always a real-image maker” be correct? Use an object position to test it.
apply.answer: No. With a real object inside the positive focal length, the outgoing rays diverge and their backward extensions form a virtual image on the object side. The sign of dᵢ captures this change.

lessons.limits: Thin lens, same surrounding medium, small angles, negligible aberrations. At dₒ=f report no finite image, not a numerical infinity in a calculation.

visual.title: Follow the physical story
visual.caption: Paraxial thin converging lens: a focal object gives parallel outgoing rays, not infinite intensity.

glossary.definition: Distance from an ideal focusing element to the focus for parallel incoming rays.

practice.prompt: A thin lens has f=12 cm and a real object at dₒ=18 cm.
practice.reasoning: 12×18/(18−12)=36 cm, positive and therefore real. The entry tolerance permits rounding; it is not measurement uncertainty.

lessons.title: A minus sign can mean upside down
lessons.idea: Transverse magnification compares signed image and object heights.
body: Choose upward height as positive for both object and image. An image tip below the axis then has negative height. This lets a sign describe orientation without a second rule.

For the thin lens, magnification is negative image distance divided by object distance. Its absolute value tells the size ratio. A value of −2 means twice as tall and inverted, not a negative physical length.
Magnification of height is not magnification of power or brightness. A larger image spreads available light differently and may also lose rays at apertures.
lessons.terms: m: Transverse magnification (no unit). Signed height ratio; |m| is the size ratio. hᵢ, hₒ: Signed image and object heights (m or cm). Use upward positive for both. dᵢ, dₒ: Signed image and object distances (same length unit). Use the thin-lens convention from the previous lesson.

equationGuide.meaning: The distance ratio gives size, and the minus sign gives orientation.

symbols.name: Transverse magnification
symbols.description: Signed height ratio; |m| is the size ratio.

symbols.name: Signed image and object heights
symbols.description: Use upward positive for both.

symbols.name: Signed image and object distances
symbols.description: Use the thin-lens convention from the previous lesson.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: Use dₒ=30 cm and dᵢ=15 cm.
A +4.0 cm object tip maps to hᵢ=−2.0 cm: half-size and inverted.

check.prompt: A lens gives dᵢ=−20 cm for dₒ=10 cm. Describe the image.
explanations: Not quite. m=−(−20)/10=+2; positive means upright.
Not quite. m=−(−20)/10=+2; positive means upright.
Correct. m=−(−20)/10=+2; positive means upright.

apply.title: Explain your prediction
apply.text: Why should you not report “magnification 2” when you calculated −2?
apply.answer: Dropping the sign loses the orientation prediction. Report a size ratio of 2 and an inverted image, or retain signed magnification −2 explicitly.

lessons.title: The first image becomes the next object
lessons.idea: A second lens acts on the ray bundle arriving from the first.
body: First find the image that lens 1 would form by itself. Then compare that location with lens 2. The second object distance is measured from lens 2, not from the original object.

If the first image lies before lens 2, rays reach lens 2 diverging from a real intermediate object. If it lies beyond lens 2, the arriving rays are already converging and the second lens has a virtual object, with negative object distance.
For lenses separated by s, use dₒ₂=s−dᵢ₁ with our left-to-right convention. Multiply the two signed magnifications to obtain the final height ratio.
lessons.terms: dₒ₂: Object distance for lens 2 (cm or m). Positive if the intermediate image lies before lens 2. s: Lens separation (same length unit). Positive distance from lens 1 to lens 2. dᵢ₁: Image distance from lens 1 (same length unit). Computed as if lens 2 were absent. m₁, m₂, mtotal: Individual and total height ratios (no unit). Signed magnifications multiply.

apply.text: Why is simply adding the two separate focal lengths not an image-location method?
apply.answer: Lens separation and the first image determine the rays entering the second lens. The second lens does not generally receive parallel rays, so its focal length alone does not locate the final image.

lessons.title: A hole can limit brightness or field of view
lessons.idea: Aperture stops and field stops restrict different ray bundles.
body: From one object point, draw a cone of rays toward the system. The aperture stop is the opening that most limits that cone. It controls how much light from that point can get through.
Now move the object point sideways. A field stop limits how far off-axis an object can be and still be seen. A camera sensor edge can act as a field stop without being the aperture stop.

The entrance pupil is the image of the aperture stop seen through optics in front of it. Its apparent size, not necessarily the physical hole size, sets the usual camera f-number for a distant object.
lessons.terms: N: F-number (no unit). A ratio, not a count of photons. f: Effective focal length (mm or m). Use the same length unit as D. D: Entrance-pupil diameter (same length unit). Apparent aperture-stop size viewed from object space.

apply.answer: Optics in front of the hole can magnify its apparent image. The entrance pupil is that image, so its diameter can differ from the physical aperture-stop diameter.

lessons.title: Acceptable sharpness needs a tolerance
lessons.idea: Depth of field is a range of object distances judged sharp enough, not perfectly focused.
body: A sensor is a fixed plane. Only one ideal object plane is exactly in focus for a chosen lens position. Other object planes form their best images slightly before or behind the sensor, leaving blur circles there.
A smaller pupil narrows each ray cone, reducing geometric defocus blur. This can increase depth of field for a chosen acceptable blur size. But the smaller aperture also increases diffraction blur.

For a simple converging cone, the defocus blur diameter is approximately pupil diameter times sensor offset divided by the focused image distance. Real camera specifications require magnification, pupil placement and a chosen viewing criterion.

Equal to pupil diameter in this simple thin-lens model. δ: Sensor offset from best image plane (same length unit). apply.text: Why should two photographers state their viewing assumptions before comparing depth of field?
apply.answer: They may accept different blur sizes because of sensor sampling, print size, viewing distance or desired detail. Depth of field includes that judgment threshold, not only the lens geometry.

lessons.title: Angular size is not image height
lessons.idea: An instrument can make an object subtend a larger angle at the eye.
body: Your eye’s optics form a real image on the retina. Accommodation changes focusing power to handle different object distances; it does not move the object itself.

A simple astronomical telescope uses an objective to make a real intermediate image, then an eyepiece to present that image under a larger viewing angle. For relaxed viewing, the emerging rays are parallel.

For two positive lenses in an ideal telescope, angular magnification is minus objective focal length divided by eyepiece focal length. A microscope also uses an objective and eyepiece, but its nearby-object geometry differs; do not reuse the telescope formula blindly.

For a simple microscope, put a nearby object just beyond the objective focal point. An objective with f=4 mm and object distance 5 mm makes an inverted real intermediate image 20 mm away, with height magnification −4. Place that intermediate image at the eyepiece’s front focal plane: outgoing rays are parallel for a relaxed eye. The eyepiece changes the viewing angle of this already enlarged image; unlike the telescope, the objective did not start with a distant object.

apply.text: Why does larger angular magnification not always reveal new detail?
apply.answer: The objective’s diffraction, aberrations and available signal already limit the information. Enlarging an unresolved blur makes a bigger blur, not newly separated detail.

lessons.title: Split a transverse field into two directions
lessons.idea: Polarization describes the direction pattern of the electric field.
body: For a plane wave travelling along the z direction in a uniform isotropic medium, the electric field lies in the perpendicular x–y plane. Its two components can change with time even while the beam travels steadily forward.
Components are signed projections, not two separate beams. Add the x-directed and y-directed field arrows to recover the actual field arrow at each instant.
A detector usually averages over enormous numbers of optical cycles. It does not follow each arrow directly, but polarizers let us infer how the field is oriented.
lessons.terms: E: Instantaneous field magnitude (V/m). Volts per metre measures electric field strength. Eₓ, Eᵧ: Perpendicular field components (V/m). Subscripts name the x and y axes; squares mean multiplication by themselves.

equationGuide.meaning: Perpendicular components combine by the right-triangle rule, not ordinary signed addition.

apply.title: Explain your prediction
apply.text: Why is a transverse optical field not the same as a charged particle moving sideways along the ray?
apply.answer: The field is a physical quantity spread through space, with a direction at each point. Its transverse direction describes the electric field, not a material particle trajectory following the oscillating arrow.

lessons.limits: Plane transverse wave in a uniform isotropic medium; tightly focused and guided fields can have longitudinal components.

lessons.title: A polarizer selects a field projection
lessons.idea: For linear polarization, transmitted power follows the square of a projection.
body: An ideal linear analyzer passes the electric-field component along its transmission axis and rejects the perpendicular component. A field at angle θ has an along-axis amplitude reduced by cosine θ.
Irradiance is proportional to amplitude squared, so the transmitted irradiance is multiplied by cosine squared. This is Malus’s law for an already linearly polarized input.
Unpolarized light does not have one fixed polarization angle. Its average transmission through a first ideal polarizer is one half; only then can you apply Malus’s law to a second polarizer.
lessons.terms: Iin, Iout: Incoming and transmitted irradiance (W/m²). In and out label before and after the analyzer. θ: Angle between polarization and analyzer axes (degrees or rad). cos²θ means (cosθ)×(cosθ).

equationGuide.meaning: The field projection is squared because the detector measures energy flow, not signed field.

apply.answer: It is largely absorbed and can become internal energy, rather than disappearing. Other polarizer designs redirect rejected polarization. Malus’s transmitted-power relation is not a complete device energy diagram.

lessons.title: A field tip can trace a circle
lessons.idea: Relative phase between perpendicular components changes polarization shape.
body: Watch the field arrow at one fixed position, not along the beam. If perpendicular components rise and fall together, the tip stays on a straight line: linear polarization.

Equal component amplitudes with a quarter-cycle phase difference make a circle. Unequal nonzero amplitudes with that phase difference make an ellipse. More general phase differences can also make ellipses.

The rotation sense depends on phase sign and the direction from which you look. State a viewing convention instead of assigning a handedness label without explanation. The field-tip circle is not a photon orbit.

One cycle corresponds to 2π radians. t: Time (s). ωt is the phase angle; sine is a quarter-cycle shifted cosine.

apply.answer: Equal amplitudes are not enough. The relative phase must also be a stable quarter cycle. Equal incoherent components or equal in-phase components have different polarization behaviour.

lessons.title: Delay one component without rotating its path
lessons.idea: A wave plate changes relative phase along two material axes.
body: A birefringent plate has different phase indices for two perpendicular polarization components. Split the input field along those axes before calculating anything.
After crossing thickness L, the components have accumulated different phases. The difference is proportional to the index difference and thickness, and inversely proportional to vacuum wavelength.

A quarter-wave plate adds a quarter cycle. Equal input components at 45° to its axes can therefore become circular. Input along just one axis stays linear, because there is no second component to compare.
lessons.terms: δ: Relative phase delay (rad). Only relative phase affects polarization shape. Δn: Difference of the two phase indices (no unit). Choose an axis order and retain its sign. L: Plate thickness (m). Distance travelled through the uniform plate. λ₀: Vacuum wavelength (m). Use the wavelength at which indices are specified. π: Circle constant (no unit). 2π radians is one complete cycle.

lessons.title: Add fields before squaring
lessons.idea: Coherent waves can reinforce or cancel because their fields add.
body: Two matching waves reaching the same point do not simply bring two independent brightness numbers. Their signed electric fields add first. The detector then averages the square of the total field.

For equal-frequency, same-polarization coherent beams, the intensity includes a phase-dependent cross term. In phase, equal beams give four times one beam’s intensity at that point. Opposite phase, they can give zero.
This local brightening does not create energy. The full interference pattern redistributes energy across space, with bright places balanced by dim places and the complete apparatus energy flow.
lessons.terms: I, I₁, I₂: Combined and separate irradiances (W/m²). Separate values mean each beam alone at that point. δ: Relative phase (rad). Zero means in phase; π means opposite phase. √: Nonnegative square root (no unit). The root of I₁I₂ has irradiance units.

equationGuide.meaning: The extra cross term keeps track of whether the fields reinforce or oppose.

apply.answer: When the cross term averages to zero under the measurement conditions, such as mutually incoherent sources or orthogonal polarizations in this simple detector model. It is not justified merely because two beams are present.

lessons.title: Count phase with optical path
lessons.idea: Equal geometric lengths can accumulate different optical phases.
body: A wave passing through material advances in phase according to how many local wavelengths fit along the route. A higher index gives more phase advance over the same physical length at fixed frequency.
For uniform segments, multiply each physical length by its index and add. This sum is optical path length. It is a phase bookkeeping distance, not an extra physical route.
Compare two paths using the optical-path difference. Extra phases from reflection or optical elements must be added separately; path difference alone is not always the whole answer.

Additional interface phases are excluded here. λ₀, π: Vacuum wavelength and circle constant (m; no unit). 2π is one cycle.

lessons.title: A tiny path difference makes bright stripes
lessons.idea: Two narrow coherent slits produce regularly spaced far-field fringes at small angles.
body: At the centre of a symmetric screen, the two slit paths are equal. Move sideways and one path becomes longer. Bright fringes occur when that difference is a whole number of wavelengths.

For screen distance L much larger than slit separationd and small viewing angles, the distance between neighbouring bright stripes is approximately wavelength times screen distance divided by slit separation.
This spacing does not say how bright all stripes are. Real slits have finite width, producing a diffraction envelope that can dim or remove some fringes.

lessons.title: Stable phase makes a stable pattern
lessons.idea: Fringe visibility measures contrast, not total brightness.
body: If the relative phase wanders during an exposure, bright and dark fringes move. Averaging can wash them out even though waves still superpose at every instant.
Visibility compares the brightest and darkest measured irradiances. Equal coherent beams can reach visibility 1. Unequal beam strengths limit visibility even with perfect phase stability.

Temporal coherence concerns phase correlation over a delay; spatial coherence concerns correlation between locations. A path mismatch or a large incoherent source can reduce the pattern in different ways.
lessons.terms: V: Fringe visibility (no unit). Between 0 and 1 for nonnegative intensities with nonzero sum. Imax, Imin: Fringe maximum and minimum irradiances (W/m²). Use the same exposure and background convention.

equationGuide.meaning: Contrast is the bright-dark difference divided by their total.

steps: A measured fringe varies from 2 to 10 W/m².

apply.title: Explain your prediction
apply.text: Would low fringe visibility alone prove that the source is incoherent?
apply.answer: No. Unequal beam intensities, polarization mismatch, stray background and detector averaging can also lower contrast. Diagnose those factors before attributing the result only to coherence.

lessons.title: A moving mirror changes the path twice
lessons.idea: In a Michelson interferometer, light travels out to a mirror and back.
body: A beam splitter sends light along two arms, and the returning beams recombine. Compare the round-trip optical paths, not just the one-way arm lengths.
Moving one mirror along its arm by distance Δx changes its round-trip path by 2Δx. In air approximated as vacuum, one full fringe cycle occurs for a mirror movement of half a wavelength.
Counting passing fringes measures a path change. It does not by itself reveal the initial absolute arm mismatch or the direction of motion unless you track extra information.

N: Number of full fringe cycles (no unit). May include a fractional cycle if phase is measured. λ₀: Vacuum wavelength (m). Assume a stable monochromatic source.

lessons.title: A reflected field can reverse its sign
lessons.idea: Reflection amplitude has a sign as well as a size.
body: At normal incidence between two transparent nonmagnetic media, the reflected electric-field amplitude is a fraction of the incident amplitude. A negative fraction means a half-cycle phase reversal.
From lower to higher positive index, that amplitude coefficient is negative. From higher to lower index at normal incidence, it is positive. This sign is needed when reflected beams interfere.
The reflected power fraction is the squared magnitude of the amplitude coefficient in the incident medium. Squaring erases the sign, so a power measurement alone does not retain the reflection phase.
lessons.terms: r: Electric-field reflection coefficient (no unit). Reflected amplitude divided by incident amplitude at normal incidence. n₁, n₂: Incident and second-medium indices (no unit). Positive real indices; both media are nonmagnetic here. R: Power reflectance (no unit). Fraction of incident power reflected; bars mean magnitude.

equationGuide.meaning: The sign tells phase reversal; the square tells reflected power fraction.

lessons.title: Count both the extra trip and the reflection flip
lessons.idea: A thin film can make reflected beams cancel at a chosen wavelength.
body: Compare the reflection from the top of a film with the beam that enters, reflects at the bottom and returns. At normal incidence the second beam travels an extra twice the film thickness inside indexn.
For an air–film–air arrangement with film index above air, the top reflection reverses phase while the bottom one does not. There is one relative half-cycle reversal.

With that one-reversal assumption, reflected constructive interference occurs when 2 nt is an odd half-wavelength in vacuum. Destructive interference occurs when 2 nt is a whole wavelength. Other substrate indices can change the reversal count and swap the conditions.

apply.answer: In a lossless arrangement, power redistributed out of reflection can appear in transmission. A condition bright in one output is not automatically bright in the other. The compared beams and output channel matter.

lessons.title: A repeating signal cannot label its own cycle
lessons.idea: One phase measurement determines path only modulo a wavelength.
body: A fringe repeats after the optical-path difference changes by one wavelength. Seeing the same brightness again therefore does not prove the path is unchanged.

Even a known cosine signal has an additional ambiguity: equal brightness can occur at two opposite phase offsets within one cycle. Measuring a second phase-shifted signal or tracking continuous motion can help determine direction and unwrap cycles.

An honest result distinguishes measured fractional phase, counted cycles and unknown starting order. Noise and missed fringes can create whole-cycle errors much larger than the small fractional-phase uncertainty.
lessons.terms: ΔOPL: Optical-path difference (m). Relative to a specified phase-zero reference. k: Unknown or counted whole-cycle order (integer with no unit). An absolute measurement must determine this integer. φ: Measured wrapped phase (rad). Chosen in a single 2π-wide interval. λ₀, π: Vacuum wavelength and circle constant (m; no unit). One complete cycle is 2π radians.

equationGuide.meaning: A fractional cycle locates you within a repeating interval, not which interval you occupy.

apply.text: Propose a measurement that helps separate a missed cycle from a small phase error.
apply.answer: Track a continuous phase history with adequate sampling, add a second quadrature channel to determine phase direction, or use an independent coarse distance measurement. Each adds information absent from a single repeated brightness value.

lessons.title: An opening is made of many wave contributions
lessons.idea: A wavefront can be propagated by combining contributions across an opening.
body: Instead of treating an aperture as one ray, imagine dividing it into many small patches. Each contributes a wave to a later observation point. Their phases depend on the travel distances.
The Huygens–Fresnel construction adds those contributions with appropriate weights. It is a wave model, not a claim that new independent light sources are physically manufactured at every point.
At some angles contributions largely agree; at others they cancel. This explains why an opening produces a spread pattern rather than a perfectly sharp ray shadow.
lessons.terms: Etotal: Combined electric-field component (V/m). Use one common observation point and time. E₁, E₂, …: Patch contributions (V/m). The dots mean continue the sum; each contribution includes its phase.

equationGuide.meaning: The observed field depends on the sum of contributions, including their signs and phases.

Correct. Local cancellation changes when the contributing parts change; total transmitted power still falls.

apply.text: Why should the secondary-wave picture not be used as an unrestricted literal source model?
apply.answer: A correct propagation construction includes boundary conditions, phase and weighting. Simply adding arbitrary spherical emitters can predict unphysical backward waves or incorrect amplitudes. It is a calculational representation of an existing field.

lessons.limits: Scalar diffraction bridge; vector boundary conditions and subwavelength apertures require electromagnetic analysis.

lessons.title: A narrow opening makes a broad pattern
lessons.idea: A single slit’s first dark direction depends on wavelength divided by width.
body: Across a finite slit, waves travelling toward an off-axis point have different path lengths. At the first minimum, pairs of contributions across the opening cancel.

For a uniformly lit rectangular slit of widtha, the first dark angle satisfiesa sinθ=λ. A narrower slit therefore gives a larger angular spread. This concerns the width of one slit, not the separation of two slits.
The central bright region extends from the negative first minimum to the positive first minimum. Its full angular width is twice the one-sided angle in the small-angle limit.

Must be no larger than a for this first propagating minimum to exist. a: Slit width (m). Positive width of the uniformly illuminated opening.

lessons.title: Fine fringes sit inside a broad envelope
lessons.idea: Two finite slits combine two-slit interference with single-slit diffraction.
body: The separation of the slit centres sets the rapid fringe spacing. The width of each slit sets the slower envelope that controls how bright those fringes can be.

For equal uniformly lit slits, the far-field pattern is a cosine-squared interference factor multiplied by a sinc-squared envelope. At zero angle the sinc ratio is defined by its limiting value 1, not by dividing zero by zero.
A missing order occurs when an interference maximum lies at an envelope zero. It is not a failure of the two-slit phase rule; it is an additional cancellation within each slit.
lessons.equation: I/I₀ = (sinβ/β)² cos²α; β=πa sinθ/λ; α=πd sinθ/λ
lessons.terms: I/I₀: Intensity relative to on-axis value (no unit). I₀ is the combined on-axis irradiance. β, α: Aperture and separation phase variables (rad). Greek beta uses width; alpha uses separation. a, d, λ: Slit width, centre separation and wavelength (m). Equal widths and illumination are assumed. θ, π: Observation angle and circle constant (rad; no unit). Set sinβ/β=1 at β=0 by continuity.

equationGuide.meaning: The envelope tells how much light is available; the fine factor tells how the two slits reinforce.

lessons.title: Many slits sharpen allowed directions
lessons.idea: A grating sends different wavelengths into order-dependent directions.
body: For equally spaced narrow slits, neighbouring contributions agree when the path difference is an integer number of wavelengths. That integer is the diffraction order.

Only orders with a sine magnitude no greater than 1 can propagate. Different wavelength-and-order combinations can reach the same angle, so a measured bright spot is not automatically a unique colour.

Illuminating more equally spaced grooves narrows ideal principal maxima. The ideal resolving power is order magnitude times illuminated groove count, under the usual uniform-grating criterion. It is not simply the total number of grooves manufactured on the device.

lessons.title: One point becomes a small pattern
lessons.idea: The point-spread function describes an optical system’s response to a point source.
body: Even a perfect lens with a finite aperture does not turn a distant point into a mathematical dot. Diffraction makes a distributed pattern on the image plane.

The point-spread function, or PSF, records how a point’s light is distributed. Aberrations and defocus can change its shape. It is an intensity pattern for incoherent imaging, not automatically the complex field response for coherent imaging.
For mutually incoherent object points in a linear shift-invariant region, add shifted PSF intensity patterns weighted by each point’s brightness. Two nearby points may then produce one blended peak.

Offsets shift the same response shape. h: Normalized point-response shape (1/m²). Here its area integral over the image plane is 1. B₁, B₂: Power delivered from the two points (W). Positive weights; full 2D area normalization is understood.

lessons.title: A bigger aperture can separate closer directions
lessons.idea: Diffraction limits the angular detail of a circular aperture.
body: A uniformly illuminated circular aperture makes an Airy pattern: a central spot with surrounding rings. Its first dark ring sets a useful scale for comparing two incoherent point sources.
The Rayleigh criterion places one point’s central maximum at the other’s first minimum. The small-angle separation is about 1.22 wavelengths divided by aperture diameter.
This is a specified resolution criterion, not a universal boundary between all possible and impossible inference. Noise, source strengths, processing and prior knowledge affect what can be estimated.

Comes from the first zero of the circular diffraction pattern.

apply.answer: Atmospheric wavefront changes, aberrations, alignment, focus and detector limitations can broaden or distort its response. Aperture alone sets an ideal limit only under the stated assumptions.

lessons.idea: Numerical aperture combines collection angle and medium index.
body: An objective accepts a cone of rays from an object point. The half-angle of that cone is measured from the optical axis to its edge.
Numerical aperture is the surrounding-medium index times the sine of that half-angle. It is not just a physical hole diameter. Immersion media can increase it by raising the index around the object.

A common lateral diffraction scale for microscopy is 0.61 vacuum wavelengths divided by numerical aperture. The exact resolution criterion and imaging coherence must still be stated; this is an introductory circular-pupil scale.

lessons.title: More pixels cannot recover every lost detail
lessons.idea: Optical resolution, sampling and contrast are separate limits.
body: The optics first form a continuous blurred image. Pixels then sample that image over finite areas. A fine pixel grid cannot restore spatial detail already removed by the optical system.

For a sinusoidal image pattern, sampling at more than twice its spatial frequency avoids the simplest aliasing ambiguity in an ideal band-limited model. Exactly two samples per cycle is a boundary, not a robust practical target.

Contrast tells how strongly the pattern modulates brightness. A pattern can be sampled densely yet be too weak compared with noise to identify. Resolution claims should state optics, sampling and signal quality.

lessons.title: A stripe pattern has a frequency in space
lessons.idea: Spatial frequency counts repetitions per distance rather than per time.
body: A fence with evenly spaced slats repeats as you walk sideways. A brightness pattern can repeat in the same way across an image. Its spatial frequency is the reciprocal of its period.

Do not confuse spatial frequency with optical frequency. Optical frequency counts electric-field oscillations per second; image spatial frequency counts broad brightness cycles per metre across a picture.
A sharper edge needs a wider range of spatial frequencies to represent it. Fine details correspond to higher spatial frequencies, which an imaging system may weaken or remove.

lessons.title: The far field sorts an aperture by phase tilt
lessons.idea: Fraunhofer diffraction connects an aperture field to its spatial Fourier transform.
body: At a far observation angle, light from different aperture positions has a nearly linear path difference across the opening. That linear phase ramp selects a spatial-frequency component of the aperture field.

A Fourier transform is a way to ask how much of each repeating pattern is present. In far-field scalar diffraction, the complex field amplitude follows that transform; measured irradiance follows its magnitude squared.
The aperture’s field amplitude and phase both matter. Two apertures with the same transmitted intensity but different phase profiles can have different far-field patterns.

Relative to the forward axis. λ: Wavelength in propagation medium (m). Links angle to aperture spatial frequency. U: Complex aperture field (field-amplitude units). Encodes amplitude and phase across the opening. F{U}: Fourier transform of U (normalization dependent). Braces denote the transform; bars mean magnitude and ∝ means proportional.

lessons.title: An optical pupil can remove detail frequencies
lessons.idea: Finite apertures limit which spatial variations survive imaging.
body: A lens can bring different angular or spatial-frequency components to different locations in a Fourier plane. A stop there can block selected components before the image is re-formed.

In coherent imaging, a simple transfer function multiplies the complex field spectrum. In incoherent imaging, the intensity transfer function is related to the pupil autocorrelation, so the two cutoffs are not interchangeable.

For an ideal circular pupil in a simple object-space model, the coherent cutoff is NA/λ₀ and the incoherent intensity cutoff is 2 NA/λ₀. These are frequency support limits, not promises of high contrast right up to the cutoff.

lessons.title: Distance decides which diffraction approximation fits
lessons.idea: The Fresnel number compares aperture size with propagation spreading.
body: Near an aperture, the curvature of travel distance across the opening still affects phase strongly. Farther away, a simpler linear phase approximation can become adequate for the pattern.

The Fresnel number uses a characteristic aperture radiusa, propagation distance L and wavelength λ. State the size convention: using full width instead of radius changes the number by a factor of four.

A number much smaller than 1 supports the Fraunhofer far-field approximation for this scale. Values near or above 1 need Fresnel propagation rather than simply projecting the far-field pattern onto a nearby screen. A lens can form a Fourier plane without an enormous free-space distance.

lessons.title: Equal thicknesses remove equal fractions
lessons.idea: Exponential attenuation models a constant fractional loss per distance.
body: Imagine dividing an absorbing slab into equal thin layers. Each removes the same fraction of the power entering it, not the same fixed number of watts. Later layers receive less power, so they remove less in absolute terms.
With a constant intensity attenuation coefficient, transmitted irradiance decreases exponentially with distance. The coefficient has inverse-length units so that the exponent is dimensionless.

This formula describes propagation loss inside the material. Surface reflection, scattering into other directions and changing absorption with intensity need separate accounting. A measured extinction coefficient may include more than absorption.

lessons.title: A guide admits particular field patterns
lessons.idea: Waveguides confine light through boundary-compatible modes.
body: A simple ray sketch of a glass fibre uses repeated total internal reflection at a higher-index core boundary. That is a useful starting picture, but it does not describe every possible field pattern.
A guided mode is a field distribution that reproduces its transverse shape as it advances, apart from phase and possible attenuation. Boundary conditions select the permitted propagation constants.

For a simple lossless step-index guide, a bound mode’s effective index lies between cladding and core indices. An evanescent tail extends into the cladding; the field is not a hard-edged line trapped entirely inside the core.

lessons.title: A steady mean signal still fluctuates
lessons.idea: Responsivity converts arriving power to mean photocurrent.
body: A photodiode can turn absorbed light into electric current. In its linear range, mean photocurrent is responsivity times arriving optical power. Responsivity depends on wavelength and operating conditions.

For independent detection events with Poisson statistics, count variance equals mean count. The count standard deviation is the square root of the mean. Four times as many detected events halves the fractional counting fluctuation.

This shot-noise bridge is not a complete detector-noise budget. Dark current, electronic readout noise, background and source fluctuations may dominate. Some light states also do not follow Poisson counting statistics.

lessons.title: One detection event transfers a frequency-linked energy
lessons.idea: Photon energy depends on frequency, not beam brightness.
body: Light can produce localized detection events with energy linked to optical frequency. A photon is a quantum of the electromagnetic field, not a tiny classical ball that secretly follows a sinusoidal path.

Wave amplitudes predict interference and propagation probabilities, while quantum descriptions account for discrete exchanges. Which calculation you need depends on the question; “wave or particle” is not a switch that turns one everyday object into another.

For monochromatic vacuum wavelength, photon energy is Planck’s constant times frequency, or hc divided by wavelength. Raising power at fixed frequency usually raises the photon arrival rate, not each photon’s energy.

check.prompt: The task is to predict a dark interference fringe. Which information must survive the model?
explanations: Power alone does not retain relative field phase, so it cannot locate destructive interference.
Focal length locates ideal images but does not specify the phase difference that creates a dark fringe.
Correct. A dark fringe is cancellation, which cannot be predicted after discarding relative phase.

lessons.title: Trace a new two-lens system without losing the reference plane
lessons.idea: Reset distances and multiply orientation changes at each stage.
body: Consider a real object 30 cm before a converging 10 cm lens. A second converging lens of focal length 8 cm sits 27 cm after the first. Find the final image relative to the second lens, not merely relative to the first.
Lens 1 gives an intermediate image 15 cm after itself. That point lies 12 cm before lens 2, so it is a real object for lens 2. The second image distance is 24 cm.
The first magnification is −0.5 and the second is −2. Their product is +1: the final image is upright relative to the original and the same height. Two inversions have cancelled.
lessons.terms: f, dₒ, dᵢ: Focal, object and image distances (cm). Real-is-positive lens convention; use one unit. s: Lens separation (cm). Measured from lens 1 to lens 2. Subscripts 1,2: Lens labels (no unit). Each distance has its own lens origin. mtotal: Total signed height ratio (no unit). Product of stage magnifications.

equationGuide.meaning: The intermediate image connects the stages; its position determines the next object distance.

options: You forgot that the second image distance starts at lens 2
You forgot to invert the image twice
explanations: Correct. The 24 cm result is measured from lens 2; add its 27 cm offset for the lens 1 reference.
This discrepancy is a distance-origin error; the paraxial example has not changed wavelength.
Orientation affects the magnification sign, not which lens defines the origin of the 24 cm distance.

apply.text: How would you test whether this calculation alone predicts the whole photograph?
apply.answer: Check aperture clipping, diffraction, aberrations, alignment and sensor placement. The paraxial image location and height are only part of the image; they do not determine brightness or sharpness completely.

lessons.limits: Thin paraxial lenses in a common medium, no aperture clipping or aberrations. Virtual intermediate objects require retained signs.

lessons.title: A changed aperture makes a trade-off, not a free upgrade
lessons.idea: Collecting more light and changing diffraction are linked through aperture size.
body: Take an ideal circular pupil viewing two faint distant points. Doubling its diameter quadruples its area, so a fixed uniform incoming irradiance gives four times the collected power.

The Rayleigh angle simultaneously halves at fixed wavelength. Under Poisson-limited detection, four times the mean count halves the relative fluctuation. These are three separate consequences of one geometric change.

Now double wavelength too. The diffraction ratio λ/D returns to its original value even though area remains four times larger. Photon count also depends on source spectrum, photon energy and detector response, so do not infer it from wavelength alone.
lessons.equation: A ∝ D²; θR ∝ λ/D; relative shot noise ∝ 1/√N̄
lessons.terms: A, D: Pupil area and diameter (m²; m). For circular pupils, area scales with diameter squared. θR, λ: Rayleigh angle and wavelength (rad; m). Use the same criterion and medium. N̄: Mean detected count (no unit). Positive Poisson mean; √ denotes square root. ∝: Proportional to (no unit). Other specified factors are held fixed.

equationGuide.meaning: One change can improve throughput and diffraction while other changed variables undo part of the gain.

steps: Start with diameter D, wavelength λ and mean count 2500.
At 2D with unchanged illumination and efficiency, mean count becomes 10000 and relative shot noise falls from 2% to 1%.
The Rayleigh angle halves; if wavelength also becomes 2λ, the angle instead returns to its starting value.

check.prompt: Diameter triples at fixed wavelength and uniform incoming irradiance. What are the ideal area and angular-scale factors?
explanations: The area factor is right, but a larger diameter narrows rather than widens the ideal diffraction angle.
Correct. Area scales as D² while the angle scales as 1/D.
Area depends on diameter squared, whereas the diffraction angle depends on the inverse first power of diameter.

apply.title: Explain your prediction
apply.text: Why must the unchanged-illumination assumption be stated in the photon-count comparison?
apply.answer: Changing source distance, spectrum, transmission or detector efficiency can alter arriving power and counts independently of aperture area. The geometric scaling is a controlled comparison, not a prediction for every real instrument change.

lessons.limits: Ideal circular clear pupil, uniform illumination, stable efficiency and Poisson-limited counts; ignores atmospheric and detector limitations.

lessons.title: Check a fresh signal from lens to detector
lessons.idea: A complete optical prediction reports geometry, wave scale and detection assumptions.
body: A converging lens of focal length 12 cm views a real object 36 cm away. Its circular clear diameter is 6.0 mm. Use wavelength 600 nm and suppose the correctly placed detector receives 4.0 μW after all optical losses.

First locate the real image and its orientation. Then estimate the angular diffraction scale using the clear diameter, not the lens radius. Finally convert the already-received power with the detector responsivity.

The three calculations answer different questions. The image location does not determine received power, and a mean photocurrent does not determine noise. State those missing pieces rather than filling them with guesses.
lessons.terms: f, dₒ, dᵢ: Focal, object and image distances (cm). Thin-lens signed convention. m: Transverse magnification (no unit). Negative means inverted. θR: Rayleigh angular scale (rad). Circular-aperture ideal criterion. λ, D: Wavelength and clear diameter (m). Convert millimetres before dividing. Iph, R, P: Photocurrent, responsivity and received power (A; A/W; W). R refers to detector response here, not reflectance.

equationGuide.meaning: Use a model chain, but do not confuse the output of one stage with an unmeasured input to another.

check.prompt: The detector moves away from the 18 cm image plane but still catches all 4 μW. What may change even if mean current stays fixed?
options: The image can blur through defocus
explanations: Moving the detector does not change the lens focal length; it changes where the ray cone is intercepted.
Defocus does not change the monochromatic light frequency, so it does not change energy per photon.
Correct. Collected power and spatial image sharpness are different quantities; a broad blur can carry the same total power.

apply.title: Explain your prediction
apply.text: List two reasons this ideal calculation would not certify an instrument ready for precise measurement.
apply.answer: The lens may have aberrations or alignment errors, and the detector may have background, saturation or readout noise. Calibration, uncertainty, sampling and the actual source conditions must be checked in addition to these ideal arithmetic results.

lessons.limits: Bounded introductory assessment, not professional optical validation or laser-safety guidance. Ideal results require the stated paraxial, diffraction and detector assumptions.
